previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis and a history of chronic abdominal pain was admitted for acute-on-chronic left-sided abdominal pain and reported melena. Her creatinine rose to 1.5 from a baseline of 1.0–1.1, consistent with prerenal azotemia due to poor oral intake, and improved with IV fluids. Evaluation revealed no active gastrointestinal bleeding—stools were guaiac-negative and hemoglobin remained stable. Abdominal pain was attributed to chronic issues including constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, portal hypertension, and cirrhosis, with no ascites on exam. Pyuria was noted, and she received a short course of ceftriaxone for a presumed urinary tract infection. She remained stable throughout admission, with no hepatic decompensation or encephalopathy. She was discharged home with improved renal function, continued home medications, and follow-up plans for GI evaluation of motility dysfunction and outpatient lab monitoring.
